bull_thesis: Orkla is a Nordic branded-consumer-goods owner that has quietly become a much better business while its shares fell about 21% from their 12-month high of NOK 131.20 to NOK 103.30 today. The operating evidence is unusually clean. Against the three-year targets set at the November 2023 investor day, Orkla has delivered 12% compound growth in underlying adjusted operating profit versus an 8-10% goal, lifted the adjusted operating margin by 1.6 percentage points from 9.0% to 10.6% versus a 1.5-2.0 point goal, and raised return on capital employed from 10% to 12.4% on the way to a 13% target. Full-year 2025 revenue was NOK 71.5 billion with adjusted operating profit of NOK 7.65 billion, and the fourth quarter of 2025 was the twelfth consecutive quarter of underlying profit growth. Most importantly, the growth stopped being purely price-led: volume and mix turned positive at 1.7% in the fourth quarter of 2025 and 2.2% group-wide in the first quarter of 2026, with every business contributing. The bull case has four legs. First, the parts are worth more than the whole and the discount is real. Roughly a quarter to a third of Orkla's value sits in a 42.7% stake in Jotun, the unlisted paints and coatings company, which earned NOK 5.24 billion of net profit on NOK 34.3 billion of revenue in 2025 at a 20.6% operating margin and grew underlying operating profit 16% in the first quarter of 2026 - a genuinely world-class asset that the market discounts heavily because it is private and not for sale. Second, the cost cycle is turning in Snacks: after two years of cocoa inflation that cut chocolate volumes by at least 10%, management guided in February 2026 that Orkla Snacks expects a favourable input-cost development in 2026, and the fourth quarter already produced 16% underlying profit growth in that business. Third, there is a real growth option that the market is not being allowed to size: the BUBS confectionery brand launched in the United States in the third quarter of 2025 and by the first quarter of 2026 was in more than 40,000 stores, with a global collaboration with H&M Beauty on top; management has refused to quantify it three quarters running, which means it is in nobody's model. Fourth, capital allocation has been executed rather than promised - the hydropower assets and Pierre Robert Group were sold in 2025, Orkla India was listed in November 2025 with Orkla retaining 75%, NOK 11.2 billion was returned to owners in 2025, and a NOK 4 billion buyback was completed on 22 July 2026 covering 37,542,917 shares, or about 3.8% of the company, at an average price of NOK 106.54 - above today's price. The balance sheet is a fortress at 1.0 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, cash conversion runs above 100%, and the declared NOK 6.00 dividend for 2025 is a 5.8% yield at today's price. The conditions that must hold: Jotun must absorb the oil-driven raw-material step-up without losing more than a tenth of its earnings; Orkla Health must stop getting worse; and the investor day on 1 December 2026 must set a credible 2027-2030 plan rather than a downgraded one.
bear_thesis: The bear case is not that Orkla is a bad business - it is that the good news is already paid for, and the near-term path gets harder before it gets easier. Start with what the screener got wrong, because it flatters the setup in both directions. The reported earnings per share of NOK 11.48 for 2025 is inflated by NOK 5.1 billion of one-off gains from selling the hydropower assets; the figure management itself reports is adjusted earnings per share of NOK 6.83. On an estimated NOK 7.4-7.6 of adjusted earnings for 2026, the shares trade near 13.7 times - a modest discount to Nestle, Unilever and Danone, and no discount at all to General Mills or Premier Foods. There is no deep-value setup here. Second, the growth engine is decelerating inside its own target period: underlying adjusted operating profit grew 17.3% in 2024, 6.6% in 2025, and just 3% in the first quarter of 2026. The 12% compound figure management quotes is carried almost entirely by the first year. The investor day on 1 December 2026 is therefore as likely to reset the growth bar downward as upward. Third, the cost backdrop turned against the company on 20 May 2026 and has worsened since. On that call management flagged upward pressure on energy, freight and packaging costs and warned that Jotun faces substantial input-cost increases from the second quarter that are expected to compress gross margins, because Jotun sources against global oil prices with its highest exposure in marine and protective coatings. Since that call the oil backdrop has deteriorated further, and management explicitly refused to size the impact - when asked directly whether it lands in the second quarter or the second half, the answer was that the picture changes every day. That unquantified margin risk sits immediately in front of the second-quarter report on 20 August 2026. Fourth, the underlying volume story is thinner than the headline. Full-year 2025 organic growth of 3.5% was overwhelmingly price; Orkla Foods' volume and mix were negative 1.1% for the year and negative in Norway again in the fourth quarter. Two positive quarters do not make a trend, and price-led growth in groceries eventually meets private label. Fifth, Orkla Health is a genuine impairment story, not a soft patch: adjusted profit fell in 2025, NOK 240 million of trademarks were written down in the third quarter with the Nutrilett brand taken to zero, three factories are being closed through the end of 2027, profit fell about 30% in the first quarter of 2026, and management admits the restructuring cost is not quantified even internally. Sixth, and structurally, the Jotun stake cannot be monetised. Orkla owns 42.7% of a family-controlled private company alongside the founding family, has never signalled any intention to sell, and calls it a core holding. A sum-of-the-parts discount that has no mechanism to close is not a mispricing, it is a permanent feature. Seventh, group return on invested capital on a reported basis is only 7.8%, weighed down by NOK 34.8 billion of goodwill and intangibles - about 39% of assets - which is the accumulated evidence of decades of paying full prices for acquisitions. Finally, the mechanical support has just been withdrawn. For eight months a company bid stood in the market for up to a quarter of daily volume; it completed on 22 July 2026 and no successor programme has been announced. What would confirm the bear case: a second-quarter report on 20 August 2026 showing Jotun's margin compressing faster than guided, another leg down in Orkla Health, or a 1 December 2026 investor day that lowers the medium-term growth ambition.
consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is narrower than the screening flag suggests, and it runs in both directions. The first and largest disagreement is with our own intake, not with the street. This name arrived tagged as deep value on the strength of a fair value of NOK 13.43, a margin of safety of negative 99% on all five models, a price-to-free-cash-flow of 160 times and a 100% gross margin. Every one of those is a data failure. Corrected, Orkla earns NOK 6.83 of adjusted earnings per share, generates NOK 7.27 billion of free cash flow, and trades near 13.7 times estimated 2026 adjusted earnings with a 5.8% dividend yield. The apparent 99% discount does not exist. Against the actual street, our genuine disagreement is about Jotun. Analysts largely treat the 42.7% stake as dead capital and apply a full conglomerate discount, and the published targets are unusually scattered as a result - one vendor puts consensus at about NOK 112, another at an average of about NOK 129 with a range of NOK 100 to NOK 160, and Danske Bank trimmed to NOK 150 with a buy rating in June 2026. That dispersion is itself the tell: the street cannot agree what Jotun is worth. Jotun is the best-performing part of the group - NOK 5.24 billion of net profit in 2025 on a 20.6% operating margin, with underlying operating profit up 16% in the first quarter of 2026 - and it is the part carrying the widest discount. We think the discount is too wide, but only modestly, because we also think the bulls are wrong about the mechanism. Orkla cannot sell this stake. It owns a minority of a family-controlled private company, has consistently called it a core holding, and has never signalled otherwise. A discount with no closing mechanism is a feature of the structure, not an arbitrage. Our second, smaller disagreement is on the direction of costs. The street has priced the cocoa relief that management guided in February 2026, but appears to have under-weighted what management said three months later on 20 May 2026: that energy, freight and packaging costs are rising, and that Jotun specifically faces substantial input-cost increases from the second quarter that will compress gross margins because it sources against global oil prices. The oil backdrop has since deteriorated further. So the market is right that Orkla is a better business than it was, right that it is not cheap, and probably too complacent about the second-quarter cost print.
forcing_function: The one genuinely dated event that could move the multiple is the investor day in Oslo on 1 December 2026, announced by the chief executive on the 12 February 2026 results call and repeated in the quarterly report. There Orkla will set its strategic direction through 2030, publish new financial targets, and present the full-potential plans its portfolio companies are currently building for the 2027-2030 period. This matters because the current three-year framework expires this year, and because the company has explicitly re-labelled itself an industrial investment company focused on brands and consumer-oriented businesses - a self-description that invites the market to value it by its parts and hints that more parts may move. Two businesses remain in the transform-or-exit bucket and management has said it has stepped up its evaluation of value-adding structural opportunities while committing to walk away from anything not in shareholders' interest. Before that: second-quarter results on 20 August 2026, third-quarter results in late October. Beyond it: the 2027 annual general meeting, which votes on cancelling the remaining 23,698,870 treasury shares, 2.4% of the capital - mechanically accretive but already public and therefore not a surprise. Note what is deliberately absent from this list. An investor day is a presentation, not a transaction; it carries no contractual terms and no fixed payout. The events that did carry real terms - the Indian listing and the NOK 4 billion buyback - have both already run their course.
valley_of_death: The risky window runs from now to roughly the end of the year, and it has four distinct components. First, and most immediate, the mechanical support has just gone. From 17 November 2025 to 22 July 2026 the company itself stood in the market buying up to a quarter of daily volume, taking in 37.5 million shares - about 3.8% of the company - at an average of NOK 106.54, which is above today's NOK 103.30. That bid completed five days ago and no successor programme has been announced. The first unsupported weeks of trading are the nearest risk. Second, the second-quarter report on 20 August 2026 carries an unquantified cost step-up. Management flagged on 20 May 2026 that Jotun expects substantial input-cost increases from the second quarter with gross-margin compression, and that the consolidated businesses face energy, freight and packaging inflation; when pressed on timing the answer was that the picture changes every day and the effect would come gradually. Jotun contributes the group's associate income - NOK 2.18 billion in 2025 - and is the single largest swing item in the quarter. Third, Orkla Health is a known and dated drag with an unknown bill. Profit fell about 30% in the first quarter of 2026, management has guided that full-year profitability will not be satisfactory, three factories are closing gradually through the end of 2027, and the restructuring cost is admitted to be unquantified even internally, including possible balance-sheet write-downs. Fourth, there is no cash-return event between here and the investor day. The NOK 6.00 dividend for 2025 was paid after the 23 April 2026 annual meeting; the next distribution is roughly a year away, and the treasury cancellation vote is not until the 2027 annual meeting. There is no cash-burn or maturity problem to fear - net debt is 1.0 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, the average borrowing cost has fallen to 4.3%, and cash conversion runs above 100% - so this is a multiple-and-sentiment window, not a solvency one. The current market regime sharpens it: with volatility cheap against a live supply shock at a key oil chokepoint, negative surprises are travelling further than positive ones, and Orkla's Jotun leg is directly in the path of that shock.
positioning_washout: There is no forced-selling dynamic to harvest here, and that is the honest answer. Orkla's register is anchored by Canica, the Hagen family holding company, with about 25% of the shares, alongside large Norwegian institutional and index holders and a broad base of Nordic income funds. Nothing in the setup forces mechanical liquidation: the dividend is intact at NOK 6.00 for 2025 including a NOK 2.00 top-up, there is no leverage problem at 1.0 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, no index deletion is in prospect, and no strategic pivot is asking a yield-focused shareholder base to reconsider why it owns the stock. The one genuine flow event in the past year ran the other way - the company itself was the buyer, and its withdrawal on 22 July 2026 removes a support rather than creating a seller. The only plausible overhang is the estate. Chairman Stein Erik Hagen, who had been on the board since 2004 and chaired it since 2006, died suddenly on 4 May 2026, putting a quarter of the register into a generational transfer. The dated evidence points to continuity, not a sale: Caroline Hagen Kjos was already running Canica, and at an extraordinary general meeting on 10 July 2026 Christer Kjos was elected Chair alongside a new board member, Jan Ole Stangeland. A family that intended to exit does not take the chair. We therefore treat an estate-driven block sale as a tail risk with no supporting evidence rather than a live overhang - but it is a variable that did not exist twelve months ago, and a change in that stance would be the single largest flow event this shareholder register can produce.
moderator_conclusion: Wait for a better price. This is a good business that has been doing what it said it would, and it is not on sale. Strip out the broken screening data and Orkla is a Nordic branded-goods owner earning NOK 6.83 of adjusted profit per share in 2025, on track for roughly NOK 7.4 to 7.6 in 2026, trading at about 13.7 times that with a 5.8% dividend yield, net debt at 1.0 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and cash conversion above 100%. The forensic record is clean: twelve consecutive quarters of underlying operating-profit growth, margin up 1.6 points and return on capital employed up 2.4 points over the strategy period, a management team that names its own weakest business unprompted, and a capital-allocation programme that was executed rather than announced. Building the value from the parts - the eight operating businesses at differentiated multiples, the 75% of the separately listed Indian business marked to its actual quote, the 42.7% of Jotun at a discount that reflects its being unlisted and unsellable, less NOK 14.2 billion of net debt including leases - gives about NOK 111 per share against NOK 103.30 today. That is roughly 8% of upside to fair value against a fifth of downside in the adverse case. It is not an entry. Three things argue specifically for patience rather than a pass. The company bought 3.8% of itself over the past eight months at an average of NOK 106.54, finished on 22 July 2026, and has announced nothing to replace it - a supportive bid has just left the market. The second-quarter report on 20 August 2026 carries a cost step-up that management flagged on 20 May and then declined to size, and the oil backdrop behind it has worsened since, which lands directly on Jotun, the group's single largest and least controllable earnings contributor. And the underlying growth rate is decelerating inside its own target window, from 17.3% in 2024 to 6.6% in 2025 to 3% in the first quarter of 2026, so the 1 December 2026 investor day is at least as likely to lower the medium-term bar as raise it. On the regime: this book is right to be wary of theses that hinge on one shared macro driver. Orkla is genuinely independent of the artificial-intelligence capital-expenditure cycle that dominates the tape, which is worth something - but it is not independent of oil, because a quarter of its value sits in a coatings business whose raw materials track crude and whose marine franchise tracks shipping. The independence credit is therefore partial, and it does not move the conviction. Nothing here depends on interest-rate relief, which is appropriate in a tape where a hike remains the priced base case. On the two catalysts: both have fired, and in this book that is neither a mark for nor against. The Indian listing completed in November 2025 and the shares have since fallen about 24% below the offer price; the buyback completed last week. We judge what is left, which is the residual value case - and the residual value case is fair, not cheap. Set a level rather than a date. We would move to a buy at NOK 92 or below, which is roughly 12 times estimated 2026 adjusted earnings and about 4% under the 12-month low of NOK 96.15, or immediately on a new capital-return programme announced with the 20 August 2026 results that restores the mechanical bid. Absent one of those, the quality here is real and the price is not yet.
sop_breakdown: Base-case parts, valuing the consolidated businesses on estimated 2026 adjusted operating profit and adding the two stakes separately. Orkla Foods Europe NOK 2.75bn of profit at 12 times equals NOK 33.0bn - the largest single part, a stable 12.6% margin business with a 14.9% return on capital employed but near-zero volume growth. Orkla Snacks NOK 1.40bn at 14 times equals NOK 19.5bn, the highest multiple among the consolidated parts because the cocoa headwind is reversing and the United States launch of BUBS is a real option. Orkla Food Ingredients NOK 1.58bn at 10.5 times equals NOK 16.6bn - the second-largest revenue base but a business-to-business ingredients distributor at a 7.1% margin, so it earns a distribution multiple. Orkla Health NOK 0.80bn at 9 times equals NOK 7.2bn, marked down for a shrinking profit base, written-off trademarks and three factory closures running to the end of 2027. Orkla Home and Personal Care NOK 0.37bn at 14 times equals NOK 5.2bn, the highest-returning business in the group at a 24.5% return on capital employed. The European Pizza Company NOK 0.40bn at 11 times equals NOK 4.4bn. Orkla House Care NOK 0.23bn at 9 times equals NOK 2.0bn. The Health and Sports Nutrition Group NOK 0.06bn at 7 times equals NOK 0.4bn. Orkla Real Estate at about book value equals NOK 1.5bn. Central costs of NOK 0.37bn a year capitalised at 10 times equals minus NOK 3.7bn. That gives NOK 86.1bn of enterprise value for the consolidated operations excluding India. Then the two stakes: the 75% of the separately listed Orkla India marked to its actual Indian quote of 556.75 rupees on 24 July 2026 is worth about NOK 5.8bn, some 24% below the November 2025 offer price of 730 rupees; and 42.7% of Jotun at 16 times Orkla's NOK 2.24bn share of 2025 net profit, less a 15% discount for an unlisted, non-controlling and effectively unsellable stake, is worth about NOK 31bn. Subtract NOK 14.2bn of net debt including NOK 2.4bn of capitalised leases as at 31 March 2026 - about NOK 11.8bn excluding leases, which is the figure the company itself tends to quote - and about NOK 1.5bn of minority interests outside Orkla India. Equity value of roughly NOK 107bn across 963.75 million shares outstanding net of 23.7 million treasury shares gives NOK 111 per share. Cross-check: that is about 11 times enterprise value to operating profit on the consolidated businesses and about 15 times estimated 2026 adjusted earnings, against a current 13.7 times.
risk_reward: Poor at this price. Downside to the adverse case sits at NOK 82 and upside to base-case fair value at NOK 111, so the shares risk roughly three kroner for every one they stand to gain on the central case; the favourable case at NOK 142 restores a positive ratio only if you underwrite both a Jotun re-rating and an Orkla Health turnaround at the same time. There is no structural floor - the 5.8% dividend and the 1.0 times leverage remove any distress mechanic but neither is a contractual downside stop, and the 12-month low of NOK 96.15 is a chart level, not a floor.
peer_comps_note: The supplied peer note reaches the wrong conclusion because it rests on a broken number. It calls Orkla expensive versus Nestle, Unilever, Danone and General Mills on a price-to-free-cash-flow of about 160 times. That figure is a data artifact: trailing free cash flow is NOK 7.27 billion against a market value near NOK 100 billion, which is about 13.7 times, and enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation is 9.7 times with a 7.2% free-cash-flow yield. On the same trailing data the vendor also reports a 100.0% gross margin - it recorded no cost of revenue for the 2025 year - which is what breaks the five valuation models that all print a negative 99 to 100% margin of safety and a fair value near NOK 13 for a NOK 103 share. None of those figures were used here. On corrected numbers Orkla is neither rich nor cheap against its peer set. At roughly 13.7 times estimated 2026 adjusted earnings and about 11 times enterprise value to operating profit on the consolidated businesses, it sits at a modest discount to the large European branded-food majors and at no discount to the cheaper end of the group. The peer note's second point stands and matters: reported return on invested capital of 7.8% does trail the branded-goods majors, because NOK 34.8 billion of goodwill and intangibles, some 39% of assets, sits in the denominator from decades of acquisitions. The counterweight is that return on capital employed on the operating businesses is 12.4% and has risen 2.4 points in two years. A conglomerate discount is therefore appropriate, and the valuation above applies one - the sum-of-the-parts is built bottom-up from Orkla's own segment profits at differentiated multiples rather than from a single peer multiple, precisely so that the answer does not hinge on a stale peer anchor.

# Orkla ASA (ORK.OL) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 27 July 2026 · **Price used:** NOK 103.30 on Oslo Børs (Oslo Stock Exchange), the company's only listing; all figures in Norwegian kroner (NOK) unless stated. *(Live quote, 27 July 2026: NOK 103.30, up 1.3% on the day; 52-week range NOK 96.15–131.20; the shares sit about 21% below their 12-month high and roughly 7% above the low.)*

**Transcripts reviewed:** five consecutive quarterly calls — Q1 2025 (9 May 2025), Q2 2025 (14 July 2025), Q3 2025 (14 November 2025), Q4/full-year 2025 (12 February 2026), Q1 2026 (20 May 2026).

**What Orkla is, in one paragraph.** Orkla is a Nordic branded-consumer-goods group that has spent the last three years reinventing itself as an "industrial investment company." It owns roughly ten operating businesses outright — Orkla Foods Europe, Orkla Snacks, Orkla Food Ingredients, Orkla Health, Orkla Home & Personal Care, Orkla House Care, The European Pizza Company, the Health and Sports Nutrition Group, a 75%-owned and separately listed Orkla India, and a small property arm — plus a 42.7% stake in Jotun, the unlisted Norwegian paints and coatings company. In 2025 the group turned over NOK 71.5 billion of revenue and earned NOK 7.65 billion of adjusted operating profit, with a further NOK 2.18 billion flowing in from Jotun and other associates.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**The story has narrowed, and that is the point.** Across these five calls management moved from "we own a lot of things and are improving them" to "we are an investment company with a defined portfolio, and here is the capital coming back to you."

*Opening frame (Q1 2025).* The emphasis was on the diversified portfolio as a shock absorber: "Orkla's positive results overall underline the benefits of a diversified portfolio." The concrete news was subtraction — Pierre Robert Group sold in March, the hydropower portfolio sold in April — framed as "we continue to simplify the portfolio." Tariffs got a full paragraph and were dismissed on the numbers (US imports and exports each under 1% of the relevant base).

*Mid-arc (Q2–Q3 2025).* Two threads took over. First, structural value release: the June 2025 draft prospectus filing for Orkla India, then the 6 November 2025 listing itself. The CEO was careful to frame it as a partial monetisation, not an exit — "this IPO is not an exit for Orkla. Orkla will remain committed — a committed major owner." Second, capital return: alongside Q3 came the NOK 4 billion buyback, funded explicitly by the India proceeds "to optimize the capital structure and return excess capital to shareholders."

*Current frame (Q4 2025 – Q1 2026).* The language turned forward. The Q4 call opened the 2027–2030 chapter: a Capital Markets Day scheduled for **1 December 2026** in Oslo, with the objective of setting "Orkla's strategic direction through 2030 as an industrial investment company focused on brands and consumer-oriented businesses." Management also raised the temperature on deals — "We have stepped up our evaluation of value-adding structural opportunities" — while immediately fitting the brake: "we are also committed to walk away from any transaction that is not in the best interest of Orkla's shareholders."

**Drivers introduced.** BUBS in the United States, first mentioned as a partnership announcement in Q1 2025, then launched in Q3 2025 and by Q1 2026 "available in more than 40,000 stores across the U.S." Cost programmes in the Sweet Ingredients cluster of Orkla Food Ingredients, which ran from Q3 2024 to completion in Q2 2025.

**Drivers quietly dropped or downgraded.** Two. Orkla Health went from a business with "significant potential" (Q2 2025) to trademark write-downs of NOK 240 million (Q3 2025) to three factory closures and a flat admission on the Q1 2026 call that its profitability "we don't expect that to be satisfactory for this year in total." And the cocoa story inverted: what was a two-year margin problem became, by Q4 2025, an expected tailwind — "Orkla Snacks expects a favorable development in input costs in 2026."

**A new risk was added late.** On the Q1 2026 call (20 May 2026) management introduced Middle East conflict effects for the first time: "we are seeing upward pressure on energy, freight and packaging-related input costs," and for Jotun specifically, "substantial input cost increases from the second quarter, which are expected to compress gross margins."

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

**The most important forensic correction.** Almost every valuation signal fed into this name by the screener is wrong. A "fair value" of NOK 13.43 against a NOK 103 share price, a margin of safety of negative 99% on all five models, a gross margin of 100.0%, and a price-to-free-cash-flow of 160 times are not judgements — they are a data-plumbing failure. The gross margin of 100% arises because the data vendor reports no cost of revenue for the 2025 fiscal year (it reported NOK 35.2bn for 2024), which then breaks every downstream model. **Nothing in this dossier or the valuation that follows relies on those figures.**

**What the returns genuinely say.** Two return measures disagree and both are real. Return on invested capital on a reported basis is 7.8% — held down by NOK 34.8 billion of goodwill and intangibles, about 39% of total assets, accumulated over decades of acquisition. Return on capital employed as the company measures it, on the operating businesses, is 12.4% and rising. The first tells you Orkla has historically overpaid for assets; the second tells you the assets it owns are being run better each year. Both are true.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising, then steady — with one honest patch of contrition.**

- **Q1 2025 — measured.** "Orkla's development for the quarter remained solid." Organic growth of 1.2% was conceded as "softer than expected." The chief financial officer presented alone; the tone was administrative.
- **Q2 2025 — the first candour.** The chief executive volunteered bad news unprompted: "Orkla Health had a weak quarter, and I'm disappointed by the development." That sentence is worth more than any guidance. Executives who name their own weakest business by name, in the opening remarks, are usually telling you the truth about the rest.
- **Q3 2025 — confident, structural.** The India listing dominates. "I'm proud of the persistence shown by our team." The buyback is announced. Language shifts from operational to capital-allocation.
- **Q4 2025 — the high point.** "I am pleased with the totality and underlying performance this quarter." Yet even here the chief executive appended: "a lot of work remains."
- **Q1 2026 — sober, with a personal weight.** The call opened with the death of Chairman Stein Erik Hagen on 4 May 2026. ## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** The operating business is measurably better than it was three years ago — margin up 1.6 points, return on capital employed up 2.4 points, twelve straight quarters of underlying profit growth, volume finally positive, the portfolio simpler by two businesses and one listing, and NOK 15 billion returned to owners over two years. Management said what it would do and did it.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** *The improvement is real and it is already in the price.* Orkla trades at roughly 13.7 times estimated 2026 adjusted earnings and about 11 times enterprise value to operating profit on the consolidated businesses, with a 5.8% dividend yield. That is a modest discount to the large European branded-food majors and no discount at all to the cheaper ones. The company has just spent NOK 4 billion buying its own shares at an average of NOK 106.54 — above today's NOK 103.30 — and that programme **finished on 22 July 2026** with no successor announced. A mechanical buyer of up to a quarter of daily volume has just left the market, five days ago, immediately ahead of a second-quarter report on 20 August 2026 that carries an unquantified input-cost step-up and Jotun's own guided margin compression. The quality is not in question; the entry price and the timing are.

**Economic moat: NARROW, trend STABLE.** The moat type is intangible-brand plus scale-in-a-small-market: Orkla owns leading local brands in Nordic grocery categories that are too small to attract global competition and too consolidated to be cheaply attacked. The evidence supports narrow rather than wide. In favour: margins expanding, returns on capital employed rising to 12.4%, market shares described as flat-to-up, and standout businesses like Orkla Home & Personal Care earning a 24.5% return on capital employed. Against: organic volume growth is roughly zero over the cycle, group return on invested capital is only 7.8% once the NOK 34.8 billion of acquired intangibles is counted, roughly 30% of revenue sits in Orkla Food Ingredients — a business-to-business ingredients distributor earning 7.1% margins, which is a distribution economics business, not a brand — and Orkla Health required trademarks to be written to zero. A wide moat does not write its brands off.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE, not terminal.** Branded packaged food faces genuine structural pressure from private label and from changing eating patterns, and Orkla is not immune — the chocolate volume decline of at least 10% shows how quickly a price-led model breaks. But there is no melting terminal base here. The categories are stable, the company is taking share in its prioritised platforms, and it has demonstrated it can reformulate, cut cost and hold profit through a severe cocoa shock (two consecutive quarters of flat operating profit in Snacks during the worst of it, then 16% growth as it eased). The nearest structural risk is cyclical-industrial rather than secular: a quarter of the value sits in an oil-input-exposed coatings business that cannot be sold.

**Is the cheapness a mispricing or a value trap?** Neither, and that is the honest answer. It is a fair price. The apparent extreme cheapness flagged by the screener is a data artifact, and once corrected, Orkla is a good, improving, conservatively financed business trading at roughly what its parts are worth. There is no melting base to fear and no deep discount to harvest.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** The operating business is measurably better than it was three years ago — margin up 1.6 points, return on capital employed up 2.4 points, twelve straight quarters of underlying profit growth, volume finally positive, the portfolio simpler by two businesses and one listing, and NOK 15 billion returned to owners over two years. Management said what it would do and did it.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** *The improvement is real and it is already in the price.* Orkla trades at roughly 13.7 times estimated 2026 adjusted earnings and about 11 times enterprise value to operating profit on the consolidated businesses, with a 5.8% dividend yield. That is a modest discount to the large European branded-food majors and no discount at all to the cheaper ones. The company has just spent NOK 4 billion buying its own shares at an average of NOK 106.54 — above today's NOK 103.30 — and that programme **finished on 22 July 2026** with no successor announced. A mechanical buyer of up to a quarter of daily volume has just left the market, five days ago, immediately ahead of a second-quarter report on 20 August 2026 that carries an unquantified input-cost step-up and Jotun's own guided margin compression. The quality is not in question; the entry price and the timing are.

**Economic moat: NARROW, trend STABLE.** The moat type is intangible-brand plus scale-in-a-small-market: Orkla owns leading local brands in Nordic grocery categories that are too small to attract global competition and too consolidated to be cheaply attacked. The evidence supports narrow rather than wide. In favour: margins expanding, returns on capital employed rising to 12.4%, market shares described as flat-to-up, and standout businesses like Orkla Home & Personal Care earning a 24.5% return on capital employed. Against: organic volume growth is roughly zero over the cycle, group return on invested capital is only 7.8% once the NOK 34.8 billion of acquired intangibles is counted, roughly 30% of revenue sits in Orkla Food Ingredients — a business-to-business ingredients distributor earning 7.1% margins, which is a distribution economics business, not a brand — and Orkla Health required trademarks to be written to zero. A wide moat does not write its brands off.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE, not terminal.** Branded packaged food faces genuine structural pressure from private label and from changing eating patterns, and Orkla is not immune — the chocolate volume decline of at least 10% shows how quickly a price-led model breaks. But there is no melting terminal base here. The categories are stable, the company is taking share in its prioritised platforms, and it has demonstrated it can reformulate, cut cost and hold profit through a severe cocoa shock (two consecutive quarters of flat operating profit in Snacks during the worst of it, then 16% growth as it eased). The nearest structural risk is cyclical-industrial rather than secular: a quarter of the value sits in an oil-input-exposed coatings business that cannot be sold.

**Is the cheapness a mispricing or a value trap?** Neither, and that is the honest answer. It is a fair price. The apparent extreme cheapness flagged by the screener is a data artifact, and once corrected, Orkla is a good, improving, conservatively financed business trading at roughly what its parts are worth. There is no melting base to fear and no deep discount to harvest.

# Orkla ASA (ORK.OL) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 27 July 2026 · **Price used:** NOK 103.30 on Oslo Børs (Oslo Stock Exchange), the company's only listing; all figures in Norwegian kroner (NOK) unless stated. *(Live quote, 27 July 2026: NOK 103.30, up 1.3% on the day; 52-week range NOK 96.15–131.20; the shares sit about 21% below their 12-month high and roughly 7% above the low.)*

**Transcripts reviewed:** five consecutive quarterly calls — Q1 2025 (9 May 2025), Q2 2025 (14 July 2025), Q3 2025 (14 November 2025), Q4/full-year 2025 (12 February 2026), Q1 2026 (20 May 2026).

**What Orkla is, in one paragraph.** Orkla is a Nordic branded-consumer-goods group that has spent the last three years reinventing itself as an "industrial investment company." It owns roughly ten operating businesses outright — Orkla Foods Europe, Orkla Snacks, Orkla Food Ingredients, Orkla Health, Orkla Home & Personal Care, Orkla House Care, The European Pizza Company, the Health and Sports Nutrition Group, a 75%-owned and separately listed Orkla India, and a small property arm — plus a 42.7% stake in Jotun, the unlisted Norwegian paints and coatings company. In 2025 the group turned over NOK 71.5 billion of revenue and earned NOK 7.65 billion of adjusted operating profit, with a further NOK 2.18 billion flowing in from Jotun and other associates.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**The story has narrowed, and that is the point.** Across these five calls management moved from "we own a lot of things and are improving them" to "we are an investment company with a defined portfolio, and here is the capital coming back to you."

*Opening frame (Q1 2025).* The emphasis was on the diversified portfolio as a shock absorber: "Orkla's positive results overall underline the benefits of a diversified portfolio." The concrete news was subtraction — Pierre Robert Group sold in March, the hydropower portfolio sold in April — framed as "we continue to simplify the portfolio." Tariffs got a full paragraph and were dismissed on the numbers (US imports and exports each under 1% of the relevant base).

*Mid-arc (Q2–Q3 2025).* Two threads took over. First, structural value release: the June 2025 draft prospectus filing for Orkla India, then the 6 November 2025 listing itself. The CEO was careful to frame it as a partial monetisation, not an exit — "this IPO is not an exit for Orkla. Orkla will remain committed — a committed major owner." Second, capital return: alongside Q3 came the NOK 4 billion buyback, funded explicitly by the India proceeds "to optimize the capital structure and return excess capital to shareholders."

*Current frame (Q4 2025 – Q1 2026).* The language turned forward. The Q4 call opened the 2027–2030 chapter: a Capital Markets Day scheduled for **1 December 2026** in Oslo, with the objective of setting "Orkla's strategic direction through 2030 as an industrial investment company focused on brands and consumer-oriented businesses." Management also raised the temperature on deals — "We have stepped up our evaluation of value-adding structural opportunities" — while immediately fitting the brake: "we are also committed to walk away from any transaction that is not in the best interest of Orkla's shareholders."

**Drivers introduced.** BUBS in the United States, first mentioned as a partnership announcement in Q1 2025, then launched in Q3 2025 and by Q1 2026 "available in more than 40,000 stores across the U.S." Cost programmes in the Sweet Ingredients cluster of Orkla Food Ingredients, which ran from Q3 2024 to completion in Q2 2025.

**Drivers quietly dropped or downgraded.** Two. Orkla Health went from a business with "significant potential" (Q2 2025) to trademark write-downs of NOK 240 million (Q3 2025) to three factory closures and a flat admission on the Q1 2026 call that its profitability "we don't expect that to be satisfactory for this year in total." And the cocoa story inverted: what was a two-year margin problem became, by Q4 2025, an expected tailwind — "Orkla Snacks expects a favorable development in input costs in 2026."

**A new risk was added late.** On the Q1 2026 call (20 May 2026) management introduced Middle East conflict effects for the first time: "we are seeing upward pressure on energy, freight and packaging-related input costs," and for Jotun specifically, "substantial input cost increases from the second quarter, which are expected to compress gross margins."

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Where said | What the numbers show | Verdict |

**The most important forensic correction.** Almost every valuation signal fed into this name by the screener is wrong. **What the returns genuinely say.** Two return measures disagree and both are real. Return on invested capital on a reported basis is 7.8% — held down by NOK 34.8 billion of goodwill and intangibles, about 39% of total assets, accumulated over decades of acquisition. Return on capital employed as the company measures it, on the operating businesses, is 12.4% and rising. The first tells you Orkla has historically overpaid for assets; the second tells you the assets it owns are being run better each year. Both are true.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising, then steady — with one honest patch of contrition.**

- **Q1 2025 — measured.** "Orkla's development for the quarter remained solid." Organic growth of 1.2% was conceded as "softer than expected." The chief financial officer presented alone; the tone was administrative.
- **Q2 2025 — the first candour.** The chief executive volunteered bad news unprompted: "Orkla Health had a weak quarter, and I'm disappointed by the development." That sentence is worth more than any guidance. Executives who name their own weakest business by name, in the opening remarks, are usually telling you the truth about the rest.
- **Q3 2025 — confident, structural.** The India listing dominates. "I'm proud of the persistence shown by our team." The buyback is announced. Language shifts from operational to capital-allocation.
- **Q4 2025 — the high point.** "I am pleased with the totality and underlying performance this quarter." Yet even here the chief executive appended: "a lot of work remains."
- **Q1 2026 — sober, with a personal weight.** The call opened with the death of Chairman Stein Erik Hagen on 4 May 2026. On the business, tone turned genuinely defensive on costs for the first time in the series — the Middle East conflict, energy, freight and packaging inflation, and Jotun's guided margin compression.

**Offensive-to-defensive shift: yes, and it is dated.** Through Q4 2025 the vocabulary was growth, volume, investment, BUBS, market share. From 20 May 2026 the vocabulary is mitigation, input costs, "this picture is kind of changing every day," and "handled through our portfolio companies." That is a real and recent change of posture, and it maps onto an oil shock that has since worsened.

**Specificity over time: stable, deliberately bounded.** Management is precise where it chooses to be (NOK 252m of Egyptian pound currency losses at Jotun; NOK 26m of Indian government incentives shifted between quarters; NOK 240m and NOK 130m of write-downs named separately) and consistently refuses quantification elsewhere. This is a disclosed policy, not drift.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: High.**

The three-year framework set at the November 2023 Capital Markets Day is the cleanest test available, because it was public, numeric, and now has two years of results against it.

| Target (2024–2026) | Promised | Delivered through 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Underlying adjusted operating profit growth | 8–10% compound | **12% compound** — ahead |
| Adjusted operating margin | +1.5 to 2.0 percentage points | **+1.6 points** (9.0% → 10.6%) — inside range with a year to go |
| Return on capital employed | 10% → 13% by 2026 | **12.4%** — on track |

Quarter-level promises also held. Cocoa: in Q1 2025 they said volumes were secured "for the majority of 2025" and that profitability would keep being hit — both proved accurate, and Q4 2025 delivered 16% underlying profit growth in Snacks as they had implied efficiency would offset. The Czech Republic warehouse disruption in Q3 2025 was promised resolved — "that's resolved at the end of Q3. So it shouldn't be impacting Q4" — and Q4 confirmed it. Jotun was guided to deliver 2025 "on par with last year," then flagged mid-year as tracking ahead; it finished with operating profit up 11% on a currency-adjusted basis.

**Sandbagging pattern: mild and honest.** Management guides to ranges it beats rather than misses, but it does not manufacture the beat — it declines to guide at all on the items it cannot control (cocoa, government grants in India, restructuring costs, deal activity). The screener's "beat 5 of 7 quarters" is consistent with a team that sets achievable bars.

**One caution.** The 2024–2026 target period ends this year and the growth rate is decelerating within it: underlying adjusted operating profit grew 17.3% in 2024, 6.6% in 2025, and 3% in the first quarter of 2026. The compound number is flattered by the first year. The 1 December 2026 Capital Markets Day will reset the bar, and the honest expectation is a *lower* growth target than 8–10%, not a higher one.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**Repeatedly deflected, in order of persistence:**

1. **Quantifying customer destocking in Orkla Foods.** Asked in Q1 2025 (Petter Nyström, ABG), again in Q2 2025 (Patrick Folan, Barclays), again in Q3 2025 (Håkon Fuglu, SEB). Answer each time: transitory, not quantified. It did in fact fade — but three quarters of refusal on a straightforward number is a pattern.
2. **BUBS United States contribution.** Asked in Q3 2025, Q4 2025 and Q1 2026. Never quantified. "We will not quantify at this moment." Analysts are trying to size the single genuine growth option in the portfolio and cannot.
3. **Marketing spend.** Asked in Q1 2025 and again in Q3 2025 (Ole Westgaard, DNB Carnegie). Answers: "slightly higher," "fairly flattish." Never a number, which makes the underlying margin improvement impossible to verify independently.
4. **Structural deals.** Asked every quarter. "We have never guided on structural deals... we will stick to that policy." Two businesses remain in the transform-or-exit bucket and the market is being asked to price an unknowable.

**Where analyst pressure preceded bad news.** Orkla Health. Ole Westgaard pushed on it in Q2 2025 ("The figures from the health segment were very weak this quarter") and got a brush-off — "I just commented upon that. So I don't think I need to elaborate more." One quarter later came NOK 240 million of trademark write-downs; two quarters later, three factory closures with costs management admitted are "not quantified internally either."

On the Q1 2026 call Petter Nyström asked directly whether the freight, packaging and energy inflation would hit in the second quarter or the second half and got: "this picture is kind of changing every day... we don't expect to see that huge effect in Q2. So this will come gradually through the year." That is an unquantified, acknowledged, forward margin risk sitting directly in front of the 20 August 2026 second-quarter report.

---

That is a modest discount to the large European branded-food majors and no discount at all to the cheaper ones. The company has just spent NOK 4 billion buying its own shares at an average of NOK 106.54 — above today's NOK 103.30 — and that programme **finished on 22 July 2026** with no successor announced. The quality is not in question; the entry price and the timing are.

**Economic moat: NARROW, trend STABLE.** The moat type is intangible-brand plus scale-in-a-small-market: Orkla owns leading local brands in Nordic grocery categories that are too small to attract global competition and too consolidated to be cheaply attacked. **Secular threat: MANAGEABLE, not terminal.** Branded packaged food faces genuine structural pressure from private label and from changing eating patterns, and Orkla is not immune — the chocolate volume decline of at least 10% shows how quickly a price-led model breaks. But there is no melting terminal base here. The categories are stable, the company is taking share in its prioritised platforms, and it has demonstrated it can reformulate, cut cost and hold profit through a severe cocoa shock (two consecutive quarters of flat operating profit in Snacks during the worst of it, then 16% growth as it eased). The nearest structural risk is cyclical-industrial rather than secular: a quarter of the value sits in an oil-input-exposed coatings business that cannot be sold.

**Is the cheapness a mispricing or a value trap?** Neither, and that is the honest answer. It is a fair price. The apparent extreme cheapness flagged by the screener is a data artifact, and once corrected, Orkla is a good, improving, conservatively financed business trading at roughly what its parts are worth. There is no melting base to fear and no deep discount to harvest.

**The self-description changed.** "Portfolio companies" gave way to "industrial investment company focused on brands and consumer-oriented businesses" (Q4 2025). That is a deliberate re-labelling: it tells you Orkla intends to be valued as an owner of assets rather than as an operator of a food company, which is an invitation to value it by its parts — and a hint that more parts may move.

**"Stepped up" is doing work.** In Q4 2025: "We have stepped up our evaluation of value-adding structural opportunities." Paired with the standing refusal to guide on deals and two businesses left in transform-or-exit, this is as close to a signal as this management gives.

Discipline is being pre-committed in public, which usually precedes either a deal at a good price or no deal at all.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** The operating business is measurably better than it was three years ago — margin up 1.6 points, return on capital employed up 2.4 points, twelve straight quarters of underlying profit growth, volume finally positive, the portfolio simpler by two businesses and one listing, and NOK 15 billion returned to owners over two years. Management said what it would do and did it.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** *The improvement is real and it is already in the price.* Orkla trades at roughly 13.7 times estimated 2026 adjusted earnings and about 11 times enterprise value to operating profit on the consolidated businesses, with a 5.8% dividend yield. That is a modest discount to the large European branded-food majors and no discount at all to the cheaper ones. The company has just spent NOK 4 billion buying its own shares at an average of NOK 106.54 — above today's NOK 103.30 — and that programme **finished on 22 July 2026** with no successor announced. A mechanical buyer of up to a quarter of daily volume has just left the market, five days ago, immediately ahead of a second-quarter report on 20 August 2026 that carries an unquantified input-cost step-up and Jotun's own guided margin compression. The quality is not in question; the entry price and the timing are.

**Economic moat: NARROW, trend STABLE.** The moat type is intangible-brand plus scale-in-a-small-market: Orkla owns leading local brands in Nordic grocery categories that are too small to attract global competition and too consolidated to be cheaply attacked. The evidence supports narrow rather than wide. In favour: margins expanding, returns on capital employed rising to 12.4%, market shares described as flat-to-up, and standout businesses like Orkla Home & Personal Care earning a 24.5% return on capital employed. Against: organic volume growth is roughly zero over the cycle, group return on invested capital is only 7.8% once the NOK 34.8 billion of acquired intangibles is counted, roughly 30% of revenue sits in Orkla Food Ingredients — a business-to-business ingredients distributor earning 7.1% margins, which is a distribution economics business, not a brand — and Orkla Health required trademarks to be written to zero. A wide moat does not write its brands off.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE, not terminal.** Branded packaged food faces genuine structural pressure from private label and from changing eating patterns, and Orkla is not immune — the chocolate volume decline of at least 10% shows how quickly a price-led model breaks. But there is no melting terminal base here. The categories are stable, the company is taking share in its prioritised platforms, and it has demonstrated it can reformulate, cut cost and hold profit through a severe cocoa shock (two consecutive quarters of flat operating profit in Snacks during the worst of it, then 16% growth as it eased). The nearest structural risk is cyclical-industrial rather than secular: a quarter of the value sits in an oil-input-exposed coatings business that cannot be sold.

**Is the cheapness a mispricing or a value trap?** Neither, and that is the honest answer. It is a fair price. The apparent extreme cheapness flagged by the screener is a data artifact, and once corrected, Orkla is a good, improving, conservatively financed business trading at roughly what its parts are worth. There is no melting base to fear and no deep discount to harvest.
